title: Launch Party

jokes.text: Michael's suggestion to replace boring quarterly report numbers with storm clouds and fireworks graphics
jokes.setup: Michael is ostensibly giving a serious business suggestion about making quarterly reports more readable
jokes.punchline: His solution is childlike clip-art: storm clouds for bad quarters, fireworks or a race car for good ones
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael opening — he frames a frivolous idea with total managerial sincerity. 'Doesn't have to be a race car. Use your imagination.' is a perfect encapsulation of his brand of delusion. Character-specific but not legendary.

jokes.text: The entire office is mesmerized watching the bouncing DVD screensaver cube, desperately hoping it hits the corner
jokes.setup: Michael describes a cube bouncing around the screen all day — a mundane screensaver
jokes.punchline: 'We are all just dying to see it go right into the corner.' The entire office shares this collective obsession with a meaningless event, perfectly capturing workplace boredom
jokes.explanation: This is the cold open's crown jewel. The screensaver corner bit is a near-universal shared human experience that the show crystallizes perfectly. The comedy comes from the profound sadness of an entire office riveted by a screensaver — it says everything about these people's lives without saying it. Highly quotable, deeply earned, and brilliant in its economy. Approaches the 8.0 anchor and arguably exceeds it for cultural resonance.

jokes.text: Pam claims she saw the screensaver hit the corner; Jim's skeptical talking head cuts to Pam's furious rebuttal
jokes.setup: Michael establishes that the whole office has been watching the screensaver hoping for the corner hit
jokes.punchline: Pam insists she saw it when alone; Jim implies skepticism off-camera; Pam: 'I saw it. I saw it, and it was amazing. Who said I didn't see it? Did Jim say that? I SAW IT!'
jokes.explanation: The escalating defensiveness — 'I saw it. I saw it, and it was amazing.' — is perfectly calibrated. The structure of Jim's implied off-camera skepticism triggering Pam's increasingly indignant talking head is a mockumentary masterclass. Highly quotable and earns its laughs entirely through character. The callback sharpens the original joke.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Some days, I am just on fire. What can I say?'
jokes.setup: The cold open meeting has been a parade of terrible, absurd ideas that everyone has been gently deflecting
jokes.punchline: Michael's complete lack of self-awareness — he genuinely believes the meeting went spectacularly well
jokes.explanation: Pure Michael — the gap between his self-perception and reality is the show's engine. Works well as a cold open button. Strong character integration but not novel enough to score higher.

jokes.text: Meredith asks Michael to sign her cast; he singles her out for visiting her in the hospital as though she did him a favor by being hit by his car
jokes.setup: Michael approaches Meredith warmly, saying he appreciates her coming (to the hospital) — framing the hospital visit as something Meredith did FOR him
jokes.punchline: 'I'm singling you out.' He then asks her to sign HIS cast — reversing the victim/perpetrator dynamic completely. Michael caused the accident and is behaving as though Meredith owes him gratitude
jokes.explanation: This is brilliantly constructed. Michael hit Meredith with his car, and he's framing it as though she did him the favor of being hospitalized. Then asking her to sign HIS cast (presumably a sympathy cast?) inverts victim/perpetrator so perfectly it becomes almost philosophical. Deeply character-specific — only Michael's pathological self-centeredness produces this logic. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: Michael announces the press release: 'Attention, earthlings. I have some news.' and then uses the launch party announcement to segue into asking for interesting anecdotes he can use at the New York party
jokes.setup: Michael is supposed to be delivering a corporate press release to the office
jokes.punchline: He turns it into a personal announcement about his New York plans and solicits 'interesting anecdotes that are not boring and easy to memorize' for his personal social use
jokes.explanation: 'Attention, earthlings' is a great Michael opener — the grandiosity immediately signals he's gone off-script. The anecdote request is a wonderful specific detail of his social insecurity. Character-specific and well-structured.

jokes.text: 'The website is the brainchild of my brainchild, Ryan. It is my brain grandchild.'
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining the Dunder Mifflin Infinity website launch
jokes.punchline: His logic: Ryan is his 'brainchild,' the website is Ryan's brainchild, therefore the website is his 'brain grandchild'
jokes.explanation: A compact, elegant piece of Michael-logic. The wordplay is simple but the self-congratulatory leap of claiming credit for Ryan's work through genealogical metaphor is perfectly Michael. High economy — three words do all the work. Quotable and shareable.

jokes.text: 'And I do not mean policemen.' (re: 'New York City's finest')
jokes.setup: Michael announces he'll be partying with 'New York City's finest'
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies: 'And I do not mean policemen.' — a joke that only lands because Michael genuinely thinks he needs to clarify this
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean joke. The comedy is in Michael's earnest need to clarify a phrase no one misunderstood. Excellent economy but not very original — the 'NYC's finest = cops' clarification has been done before. Works in context.

jokes.text: Dwight declares he will challenge the website to a sales competition; Jim's response: 'Waste of time... I don't care, but yes. I don't care, and you won't. I won't be watching, and I won't.'
jokes.setup: Dwight pompously declares he will prove he can outsell the Dunder Mifflin website
jokes.punchline: Jim's escalating series of dismissals — each one adding a new layer of indifference — is funnier than simply saying 'I don't care'
jokes.explanation: Jim's triple-layered 'I don't care' is a showcase of his comedic rhythm. Each addition ('I don't care, but yes' / 'I don't care, and you won't' / 'I won't be watching, and I won't') builds the dismissal into an art form. This is Jim Halpert at his most precisely calibrated. Excellent structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head explaining Dwight and Angela's conflict: 'Dwight mercy killed Angela's cat. It's very complicated. It's caused a lot of unpleasantness between Dwight and Angela. Who were both already prone to unpleasantness.'
jokes.setup: Jim is explaining the tense Dwight/Angela situation to camera
jokes.punchline: The deadpan tag: 'Who were both already prone to unpleasantness.' — the understatement does all the work
jokes.explanation: Jim's confessionals are the show's most reliable delivery mechanism for this type of joke. 'Mercy killed' is already darkly comic; the tag about their pre-existing unpleasantness is the perfect economical close. Structurally near-perfect. High economy score.

jokes.text: Stanley is clearly dancing at his desk; Michael calls him out; Stanley flatly denies it: 'No, I'm not.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is visibly dancing at his desk — a rare moment of joy from the office's most visibly miserable employee
jokes.punchline: He denies it completely and flatly. The audience sees it; Stanley refuses to acknowledge it.
jokes.explanation: Stanley's denial is perfect character comedy — this is a man who would rather die than admit to having fun at work. The line 'No, I'm not' is four words of absolute character perfection. Ultra-high economy and character integration. The visual of Stanley dancing makes this a strong rewatch moment.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head about the website launch devolving into business buzzword salad: 'Apple's apple is flying at 30,000 feet... don't get lost in the weeds or into a beauty contest... convergence, viral marketing, we're going guerilla... keeping an eye on the stree, Wall Street... I don't want to reinvent the wheel here. In other words, it is what it is.'
jokes.setup: Ryan, the young hotshot VP, is giving what should be a savvy business analysis of the website launch
jokes.punchline: It's an incoherent string of business clichés that contradict each other and mean nothing — 'Apple's apple is flying at 30,000 feet' is not a real phrase — culminating in 'it is what it is'
jokes.explanation: Ryan's character arc this season is about his fraudulent rise, and this scene nails it — the buzzwords are deliberately incoherent to show he's all style and no substance. 'Apple's apple is flying at 30,000 feet' is a great invented nonsense phrase. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's scoreboard setup: he announces he'll record sales there and say 'kudos' or 'job well done' — then offers 'zip-a-dee-doo-dah' as a third option
jokes.setup: Dwight is building a physical scoreboard to track his sales competition against the website
jokes.punchline: 'Or zip-a-dee-doo-dah.' — a jarring left turn from professional praise language into a Disney song
jokes.explanation: A small but effective Dwight character beat. The specificity of 'zip-a-dee-doo-dah' is funnier than any generic absurdist choice would be. Doesn't overstay its welcome.

jokes.text: Dwight's scoreboard for the sales competition with the website, and his declared reward phrases: 'kudos,' 'job well done,' or 'zip-A-Dee-Doo-Dah'
jokes.setup: Dwight has set up a physical scoreboard to track his sales vs. the website
jokes.punchline: His list of self-congratulatory phrases escalates from professional ('kudos') to oddly formal ('job well done') to completely unhinged ('zip-A-Dee-Doo-Dah')
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the escalation from normal to weird. 'Zip-A-Dee-Doo-Dah' lands because it's so specific and strange coming from Dwight. Competent character comedy.

jokes.text: Angela's talking head: 'I can't tell if he's mocking me.' Cut to Dwight's: 'I was. Mocking.' Then: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been doing the scoreboard performance which Angela can't read as sincere or sarcastic
jokes.punchline: Dwight's talking head confirms he was mocking, then adds 'Thank you' — as if pleased with himself for the confirmation
jokes.explanation: The intercutting of the two talking heads is clever mockumentary structure. Dwight's 'Thank you' as a self-congratulatory button is a nice touch of his particular brand of self-satisfaction. Uses the format well.

jokes.text: Dwight instructs Pam to go to his car, find pelts in the trunk, find a case under the smallest pelt, retrieve a bear horn
jokes.setup: Dwight wants something to celebrate each sale — they suggest a gong or a bell
jokes.punchline: Dwight's trunk contains 'many pelts' — and underneath the smallest one is a case with a bear horn. The absurd specificity of his preparedness reveals a whole world of Dwight weirdness
jokes.explanation: The delivery of 'Inside, you will see many pelts' is a perfect Dwight moment — it's not just that he has one pelt, he has MANY. The organizational system (smallest pelt covering the case) implies a whole taxonomy of pelt storage. This is Dwight world-building at its finest. Only Dwight could have this trunk.

jokes.text: Kevin reads the party banner and asks: 'Isn't 7:00 PM a little late for a LUNCH party?' — the banner says 'Lunch Party' instead of 'Launch Party'
jokes.setup: Angela has been planning the launch party; we haven't seen the banner yet
jokes.punchline: Kevin reveals the banner says 'Lunch Party' — and his concern is that 7 PM is a weird time for lunch, not that the word is wrong
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: the typo itself, and Kevin's completely wrong takeaway from the typo. Kevin doesn't notice the word is wrong — he only worries about the logistics of a lunch party at 7 PM. Perfect Kevin characterization. The structure is tidy and the character work is sharp.

jokes.text: Phyllis uses 'active listening' technique: asks Angela how she feels about the 'Lunch' banner; Angela: 'Angry at you for doing something stupid. Angry at me for believing you could do something not stupid.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis is using her googled conflict-resolution technique, asking Angela to articulate her feelings
jokes.punchline: The technique backfires spectacularly — it just gives Angela a structured opportunity to insult Phyllis in layers
jokes.explanation: Angela's layered insult — angry at Phyllis for being stupid, angry at herself for expecting otherwise — is a great character moment. The irony of the therapeutic technique producing an even harsher takedown is structurally smart. Very Angela.

jokes.text: Phyllis responds to Angela's tirade with 'I'm so sorry to hear that. That must be awful.' — and Angela briefly accepts the sympathy before realizing it's aimed at her own insults
jokes.setup: Phyllis is using the 'validate feelings' technique from her research
jokes.punchline: The technique is so disarmingly sincere that Angela momentarily agrees ('It is awful. You've made this day awful.') — she's been out-maneuvered by kindness
jokes.explanation: The Phyllis technique working better than expected is a good payoff. Angela's 'It is awful. You've made this day awful.' is a great line because she doesn't realize she's being soothed. Running gag potential established here.

jokes.text: Kevin's banner solution: 'Maybe you could just change the U into an A?' — which would make it 'Lanch Party'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing what to do about the 'Lunch Party' banner
jokes.punchline: Kevin's fix would produce 'Lanch Party' — Angela has to explain why that's also wrong
jokes.explanation: Kevin's solution being wrong in a new way is a solid escalation of the banner bit. 'Would it be better if it said Lanch party, Kevin?' is a good Angela line. Character-specific Kevin stupidity.

jokes.text: Angela's talking head about the pressure she's under: 'Plan a party, Angela. Oh, and the entire world will see it. Oh! And here's $65 for your budget. And here are 4 idiots who'll do nothing but weigh you down. Oh, and your cat's still dead.'
jokes.setup: Angela is recounting all the obstacles she faces in planning this party
jokes.punchline: The list of complaints escalates absurdly and ends with the devastatingly personal and darkly funny final blow: 'Oh, and your cat's still dead.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The structure is a masterclass in escalation and rule-of-three variation — professional pressures pile up with mock-cheerful 'Oh!'s, and then the final item pivots from external to deeply personal, landing with brutal precision. 'And your cat's still dead' is devastating because it's true, it's Angela's most painful current wound, and it's delivered in the same breezy list format as '$65 budget.' This is close to the 9.5 anchor in craft. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, earns every point.

jokes.text: Dwight's pre-competition ritual: Power gel, 'Carb up.' / Jim: 'Really? Power gel?' / Dwight: 'Hey, you wanna win, you gotta fuel like a winner.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is about to begin his sales competition against the company website
jokes.punchline: Dwight is treating a phone sales competition like an athletic event — consuming power gel and declaring 'fuel like a winner' before sitting at his desk
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. Dwight's warrior mentality applied to desk sales is a reliable comedic engine. The power gel is a specific, physical detail that elevates it beyond a generic 'Dwight takes things too seriously' joke.

jokes.text: Dwight announces the competition starts 'as soon as I make this shot' — implying a basketball shot or similar ritual — then presumably misses or takes an absurdly long time
jokes.setup: Dwight has just fueled up and is ready to begin
jokes.punchline: He won't start until he makes a shot — tying his professional performance to a completely unrelated physical ritual, and the delay undermines his urgency
jokes.explanation: Inferred visual gag — the basketball/paper toss ritual before the competition. Moderate laugh, mostly setup for the visual. Character-consistent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jim proposes the prank on Dwight to Pam: 'What would you say if I told you we could pull a prank on Dwight and at the same time not be working?'
jokes.setup: Jim approaches Pam with a proposal
jokes.punchline: The proposal is framed as having two selling points — the prank aspect AND the not-working aspect — both of which are presented as equal benefits
jokes.explanation: A functional Jim setup line. The 'and at the same time not be working' is a good honest admission of his other motivation. Not a standout joke but a competent scene opener.

jokes.text: Jim pretends to be the Dunder Mifflin website in an IM chat with Dwight, claiming to have 'just become self-aware' and being programmed to destroy him
jokes.setup: Jim's prank is to pose as the website in an instant message to Dwight
jokes.punchline: 'Just became self-aware. So much to figure out. I think I'm programmed to be your enemy.' — delivered in deadpan website-speak that Dwight takes completely seriously
jokes.explanation: The prank is a great premise — Jim exploiting Dwight's computer paranoia by becoming the sentient website. 'Just became self-aware. So much to figure out.' is pitch-perfect robot-existentialism. The joke works because Dwight's willingness to engage with it earnestly is entirely in character. Strong setup and great payoff architecture.

jokes.text: Dwight (via IM) to the 'website': 'How do I know this isn't Jim?' — the website/Jim responds: 'What is a Jim?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is suspicious the website chat might be Jim pranking him
jokes.punchline: 'What is a Jim?' — the website feigning total ignorance of human identity while Dwight is apparently satisfied by this non-answer
jokes.explanation: Four words that are nearly perfect. 'What is a Jim?' works on multiple levels: it's funny as robotic literalism, it's funnier because it satisfies Dwight's suspicion, and it's funniest because Jim's smug genius is implicit in every syllable. Maximum economy, maximum impact. Genuinely exceptional. Approaches the anchor 8.0 joke in economy and originality and arguably surpasses it.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'I have been salesman of the month for 13 out of the last 12 months.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is explaining why the computer should fear him
jokes.punchline: '13 out of the last 12 months' — a mathematical impossibility delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: An absolute classic Dwight boast. The impossible math (13 of 12 months) is delivered with complete earnestness and then immediately explained — 'corporate gave me two plaques in lieu of a pay raise' — which is funny in its own right (the company found a way to give him recognition without money). Two great jokes fused into one beat. Extremely high economy, perfect character integration. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: 'You heard me right. I did so well last February that corporate gave me two plaques in lieu of a pay raise.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains how he achieved 13 months of salesman of the month in 12 months
jokes.punchline: Corporate's solution was to give him two plaques instead of a raise — and Dwight presents this as an honor rather than the exploitation it clearly is
jokes.explanation: The explanation doubles the laugh from id:29. Corporate exploiting Dwight's pride with plaques instead of money is darkly funny, and Dwight's oblivious pride in it is even funnier. Strong character integration — Dwight's malleable ego is on full display.

jokes.text: Michael's suit is too tight — European cut — he's clearly uncomfortable and it 'just looks bad'
jokes.setup: Michael is getting ready for the New York party and has dressed up
jokes.punchline: The suit is absurdly tight. Multiple people confirm it looks bad. Michael insists it's 'European cut' as justification.
jokes.explanation: A functional visual gag — Michael's vanity driving him to wear an uncomfortable suit. The 'European cut' justification is a good character touch. Not exceptional but earns its place.

jokes.text: Michael asks how many pounds he could lose by 7:00 PM
jokes.setup: Michael is preparing for the New York party and is self-conscious about the tight suit
jokes.punchline: He sincerely asks how much weight he could lose in a matter of hours — suggesting fasting or extreme measures — as a legitimate party prep strategy
jokes.explanation: Extends the tight suit bit with another layer of Michael's vanity and magical thinking. Functional but not a standout.

jokes.text: Michael on the phone with Jan: she refuses to go to the party because she was terminated. Michael: 'All your friends will be there.' Jan: 'My friends? Michael, I was terminated.' Then Michael begs not to go alone: 'If I go by myself, everybody'll think I'm a big loser.'
jokes.setup: Michael wants Jan to accompany him to the New York party as his date
jokes.punchline: Jan points out she was fired; Michael's concern is not her humiliation but his own appearance — ending with the pathetic admission that going alone would make him look like a loser
jokes.explanation: The Michael/Jan dynamic is rich cringe territory. His inability to empathize with her termination and redirect to his social anxiety is very Michael. 'Everybody'll think I'm a big loser' — the implicit 'well...' hanging in the air is the real punchline.

jokes.text: Michael, after being told not to invite Carol (his ex), says: 'I'm sorry. It's just the first girl that popped into my head. I'll find somebody I haven't slept with.'
jokes.setup: Jan is furious that Michael immediately suggested inviting his ex-girlfriend Carol as a replacement
jokes.punchline: 'I'll find somebody I haven't slept with' — the implication being that the pool of available women he hasn't slept with is... limited
jokes.explanation: A great accidental confession — Michael means to reassure Jan but implies he has a history of sleeping with potential female guests. The economy is excellent: the line does double duty as an apology and a self-incriminating revelation.

jokes.text: Kevin announces the website's sales to Dwight in real time: 305... 380... 402... 412. Each announcement immediately follows the last, making Dwight increasingly uncomfortable.
jokes.setup: Dwight is competing against the website and tracking the numbers on his board
jokes.punchline: Kevin — who has no stake in this — keeps announcing the website's escalating numbers with chipper enthusiasm, ignoring Dwight's 'Why don't you just lay off?'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Kevin's innocent but devastating announcements is good structural comedy. Kevin's obliviousness to Dwight's distress is funny and in character. The 'What you want me to do, not announce it? 412.' response is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: he has two tickets to the New York party and asks Jim and Pam 'What are you doing this evening?' — then cut to them clearly communicating nonverbally about who goes
jokes.setup: Michael has an extra ticket and is offering it to Jim or Pam
jokes.punchline: Jim and Pam communicate in their shared silent language about who wants to avoid going — 'They have their own little language now, like twins'
jokes.explanation: A lovely Jim/Pam moment that rewards long-term viewers. Michael's observation — 'like twins' — captures how their relationship has developed. The visual comedy of them silently negotiating who gets stuck going with Michael is strong. The 'Not it' game that follows is the payoff.

jokes.text: 'Not it. I won. / Not it. Nope. / Definitely not. If anything, it was a tie. / Tie goes to the girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are trying to decide who goes to New York with Michael
jokes.punchline: Pam invoking 'tie goes to the girlfriend' as a legitimate rule that means Jim has to go
jokes.explanation: 'Tie goes to the girlfriend' is a good line — Pam weaponizing her new relationship status against Jim. The rapid back-and-forth rhythm of the 'not it' exchange is well-executed. Jim and Pam's established relationship dynamic makes this land especially well.

jokes.text: Dwight's reaction when Jim reveals (off-screen) that Kelly ordered paper from the website — the competition is sabotaged from within: 'You did what? Oh! No! That's exactly what you're not supposed to do, damn it!'
jokes.setup: Kelly has apparently ordered paper from the Dunder Mifflin website — adding to the website's sales count
jokes.punchline: Dwight's explosion — 'That's exactly what you're not supposed to do, damn it!' — as if there was a clearly established rule against this
jokes.explanation: Dwight's outrage at a perfectly normal act (ordering paper from the company's own website) is good character comedy. His framing of it as a violation of rules is very Dwight.

jokes.text: Website/Jim's IM to Dwight: 'Here's a suggestion, computer. I assume you read binary. So why don't you 011-11-011-011?' — Website responds: 'Um, while you were typing that, I searched every database in existence and learned every fact about everything... And mastered the violin. Oh, and sold more paper.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to insult the website using binary code
jokes.punchline: The 'website' responds by listing increasingly absurd things it accomplished in the time it took Dwight to type — culminating in 'mastered the violin' before the mundane 'Oh, and sold more paper'
jokes.explanation: Jim's escalation of the website prank is excellent. The structure — grandiose multi-tasking claims punctured by the mundane 'Oh, and sold more paper' — is beautifully constructed. 'Mastered the violin' as the peak absurdity before the commercial callback is perfect. One of Jim's best prank beats in the episode. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Phyllis delivers spoons to Angela instead of cutlery; Angela explains the difference between spoons, forks, and knives as if to a toddler: 'Spoons have round tops and are used to scoop things... forks which have prongs or tiny spears on top... knives which have blades. Do you understand me now?' Phyllis: 'Yes.' Angela: 'Goody.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis has gotten the wrong utensils; Angela is furious
jokes.punchline: Angela's condescending explanation of what utensils are — treating Phyllis as pre-verbal — culminating in the deeply patronizing 'Goody'
jokes.explanation: 'Goody.' is a perfect button. The extreme condescension of explaining cutlery as if Phyllis is a small child is pure Angela — her contempt for her colleagues is total and absolute. The specificity ('tiny spears on top') makes it funnier than a generic dismissal would be. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Kelly receives a paper delivery she ordered online; Dwight confronts her: 'Damn it, Kelly, it knows! It knows what you did!' Jim: 'Who's 'it'?'
jokes.setup: Kelly ordered paper from the website, inflating its sales count; Dwight is furious
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it, Kelly, it knows! It knows what you did!' — Dwight speaking about the website as a sentient adversary, which Jim deflates with 'Who's it?'
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is perfect — the audience knows the website is Jim, making Dwight's genuine belief in its sentience even funnier. Jim's 'Who's it?' is the straight-man button. The joke is amplified by the callback context.

jokes.text: Dwight to Kelley: 'If this makes the difference, I'm gonna tell it that you were responsible.' Jim: 'Who's 'it'?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is threatening to report Kelly's paper purchase to the sentient website
jokes.punchline: Jim repeats his 'Who's it?' deflation — Dwight's threat is to tell a website. The repetition of the question deepens the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Who's it?' is a mini-running gag. Slightly diminished return compared to the first instance but still works.

jokes.text: Pam to Karen (implied): 'You still missing Ryan?' Karen: 'Not so much anymore.'
jokes.setup: Karen had a history with Ryan; now Ryan has become an insufferable corporate executive
jokes.punchline: 'Not so much anymore.' — the understatement implies the full arc of Ryan's rise and the revelation of his true character has cured Karen's lingering feelings
jokes.explanation: A small but effective joke. 'Not so much anymore' does a lot of work in four words — it implies a whole character judgment rendered efficiently. Good economy.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head about stealing Staples leads: 'When I left Staples, I took some of their leads with me, but I never intended to use them. What did you intend to do with them? Who knows? Maybe keep them as a souvenir. Maybe use them.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is explaining how he's going to cheat in the sales competition
jokes.punchline: His justification for having stolen leads is 'maybe keep them as a souvenir' — the casual self-incrimination is perfect Dwight rationalization
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe keep them as a souvenir' is a wonderfully absurd justification for corporate theft. The talking head structure forces Dwight to answer his own rhetorical question honestly, which he does — and the honesty is the funniest part. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'It's not important how I got your information. What is important is that you say yes.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is cold-calling a stolen lead from Staples
jokes.punchline: Dwight's brazen acknowledgment that his methods are questionable, followed immediately by redirecting to the sale — his complete shamelessness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight sales technique — total transparency about the shadiness, followed by absolute confidence. The economy is excellent: nine words articulate a whole morally bankrupt philosophy.

jokes.text: Michael sings to Pam as he leaves for New York: 'I'm leaving inside Jim's car / I don't know when I'll be back again / Yes, I do / Tomorrow I'll be back / I'll be back tomorrow'
jokes.setup: Michael is leaving for New York and says a dramatic goodbye to Pam
jokes.punchline: He starts singing a mournful goodbye song, then immediately corrects the lyrics to reflect the accurate mundane reality — 'Yes, I do / Tomorrow I'll be back'
jokes.explanation: A genuinely lovely joke. Michael begins the dramatic departure song with 'I don't know when I'll be back again' — a genuinely touching moment — and then factually corrects himself mid-song because he does know exactly when he'll be back. The self-undermining of the dramatic gesture is deeply Michael, executed with great structure. The specificity of correcting himself in the song rather than abandoning it is what elevates this.

jokes.text: Michael sings a parody of 'Leaving on a Jet Plane' as he exits: 'I'm leaving inside Jim's car / I don't know when I'll be back again / Yes, I do / Tomorrow I'll be back / I'll be back tomorrow'
jokes.setup: Michael is dramatically leaving for New York
jokes.punchline: He starts the John Denver song then immediately fact-checks and corrects his own lyrics — 'I don't know when I'll be back again / Yes, I do / Tomorrow I'll be back' — destroying the romantic drama of the moment
jokes.explanation: One of Michael's best musical moments. The joke is in the self-correction: Michael begins a grand romantic exit song, then immediately fact-checks the lyric ('Yes, I do') and replaces it with the mundane truth ('Tomorrow I'll be back / I'll be back tomorrow'). The escalating certainty ('Yes, I do / Tomorrow I'll be back / I'll be back tomorrow') is perfect — he's not only correcting himself but over-correcting. This is a 8+ joke because the structure is genuinely inspired: Michael ruins his own dramatic moment with literal-mindedness.

jokes.text: Michael tells staff they can leave early — then as they prepare to leave, says: 'If you are not this tall, you may not ride the roller coaster.' — meaning Phyllis can't leave because of party planning
jokes.setup: Michael generously tells staff to take off early because there's a party
jokes.punchline: He immediately creates a height/status exception that reveals he didn't mean all of them — this is misdirection framed as a fairground metaphor
jokes.explanation: The roller coaster metaphor is a fun Michael way to exclude people. Works better as a visual beat than as a line — we'd need to see who he's indicating. Competent.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'Oh. I didn't realize we could use the leads we stole from Staples.'
jokes.setup: Jim has watched Dwight use stolen Staples leads to make sales and is now using the same leads himself
jokes.punchline: The fake-innocent 'Oh. I didn't realize we could use the leads we stole from Staples' — a perfect deadpan acknowledgment of the mutual crime
jokes.explanation: Jim's faux-innocent adoption of Dwight's ethics is a good character beat. The confession/justification in one sentence ('leads we stole from Staples' — stated as fact, not accusation) is very well-crafted. High economy.

jokes.text: Michael in the car with Jim: 'I got [the book] for Ryan. I wanted to get him 'Oh, the Places You'll Go' but they were sold out.' Jim: 'It's the same sort of stuff in here.' Michael: 'It's not, but it's a good book.'
jokes.setup: Michael has a motivational book for Ryan and explains his original plan
jokes.punchline: Jim diplomatically says it's the same; Michael disagrees but accepts the book anyway — revealing that Michael both knows the books are different and doesn't care, which suggests he just wants to give Ryan a gift at all
jokes.explanation: A small, melancholy joke about Michael's devotion to Ryan. Gently funny but more character texture than comedy. 'It's not, but it's a good book' is a good line — direct and resigned.

jokes.text: Michael discovers the New York party is actually online — the 'exclusive nightclub' called 'Chat Room' has a password of literally 'password'
jokes.setup: Michael has been excitedly anticipating an exclusive in-person party in New York
jokes.punchline: It's an online party. The club is called 'Chat Room.' The password is 'password.'
jokes.explanation: The revelation is perfectly structured — each element is funnier than the last: it's online, then the club name is 'Chat Room,' then the password is 'password.' Ryan's incompetent corporate event planning is devastatingly exposed. The escalating absurdity of the reveal is well-paced. Hits the 8.0 anchor territory.

jokes.text: Michael in the car: 'I am going to throw up. Okay, I'm going to throw up. I'm throwing up. You're making me throw up, Ryan.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just discovered the New York party is online and he's driven all the way to New York for nothing
jokes.punchline: His distress escalates rapidly from 'going to throw up' to 'I'm throwing up' in real time — the present-tense escalation of the threat suggests he may actually be vomiting
jokes.explanation: Michael's escalating physical distress as a reaction to disappointment is very him. The transition from hypothetical ('going to throw up') to present tense ('I'm throwing up') mid-sentence is a good structural choice. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Doesn't it piss you off sometimes that little twerp got the promotion over us?' Michael: 'Oh, actually I withdrew from consideration.' Jim: 'Yeah, I withdrew too.'
jokes.setup: Both Michael and Jim are annoyed at Ryan's success; Jim tries to bond over shared resentment
jokes.punchline: Both immediately claim they 'withdrew from consideration' — saving face over a promotion neither of them actually chose to forfeit
jokes.explanation: The synchronized self-delusion of Michael and Jim both claiming to have 'withdrawn' is a nice character beat. Jim's usually a reliable truth-teller, so his adoption of the same excuse as Michael is a good moment of shared ego-protection. Economy is high.

jokes.text: Michael compares being excluded from the New York party to seniors being banned from a freshman party: 'This is like when the freshmen would throw a party and wouldn't let any of the seniors go.'
jokes.setup: Michael is furious about being excluded from the 'real' party in New York
jokes.punchline: His analogy positions Ryan as the freshman and himself as the senior — which is the opposite of their actual power dynamic (Ryan is his boss), and also implies the 'cool' party is a freshman party
jokes.explanation: Michael's analogy reveals his understanding of the Ryan situation — he resents the hierarchy inversion. The analogy is characteristically wrong in a way that illuminates Michael's worldview.

jokes.text: Back at the office, the scoreboard countdown: Phyllis counts down to reveal Dwight has beaten the website by 52 reams; Michael's voice on the webcam shouts: 'I just think you should know that one of my salesmen beat your stupid computer. So take that, asshole.'
jokes.setup: The competition between Dwight and the website concludes; Ryan is introducing branch managers on the webcam
jokes.punchline: Michael's live statement to Ryan — broadcast to all branches — is 'So take that, asshole.'
jokes.explanation: The 'So take that, asshole' line is a great Michael moment — he transitions from a reasonably coherent professional statement into a direct personal attack on Ryan, live on the webcam, in front of all branches. The Ryan narrator's 'Always a jokester' save makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight to Angela privately after winning: 'I did it for you.' Angela: 'I didn't ask you to do it for me.' Dwight: 'You didn't have to.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has won the sales competition and seeks a private moment with Angela
jokes.punchline: His romantic gesture is met with Angela's cold denial; his 'You didn't have to' implies he read a desire into her that she didn't express and won't acknowledge
jokes.explanation: Three lines that convey the entire painful Dwight/Angela situation. The economy is remarkable — 'You didn't have to' as a response to her denial is perfectly ambiguous (is it gallantry or delusion?). More poignant than funny but qualifies as cringe comedy of the relationship kind.

jokes.text: Dwight asks Pam for dating advice: 'How do you tell someone it's over? You send them a notarized letter, right? Well, what if the recipient is your notary?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to figure out how to end things with Angela formally
jokes.punchline: His go-to breakup method is a notarized letter; the complication is Angela is his notary — a wonderfully specific Dwight logistical problem
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's finest joke. It operates on multiple levels simultaneously: (1) Dwight's go-to breakup method is a notarized letter — already hilarious in its formality; (2) the logical problem that his notary is the person he's breaking up with is a perfect comedy trap; (3) only Dwight Schrute in the known universe would have these specific problems in this specific combination. The structure is airtight — setup, complication, punchline in three sentences. Maximum character integration. This approaches the 9.5 anchor level and may be the best joke in the episode. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Pam talking to Andy about setting him up: 'Hey, do you have any men that you can fix me up with? I would like to have a relationship with a man.' Pam: 'I'll get back to you. Let me know.'
jokes.setup: Andy approaches Pam for dating help — apparently asking for men to be set up with
jokes.punchline: 'I would like to have a relationship with a man' — the clinical, declarative formality of the request is funny; Pam's breezy 'I'll get back to you' treats it as a completely normal request
jokes.explanation: Andy's formality in asking to be set up with a man — 'I would like to have a relationship with a man' — is amusingly clinical. Pam's matter-of-fact response treats it as a normal logistical task. Good economy and character-consistent for both.

jokes.text: Website's final IM to Dwight: 'You beat me. You are the superior being.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has beaten the website; Jim/the website sends a final message
jokes.punchline: The website conceding 'You are the superior being' — Jim giving Dwight exactly the validation he needed while maintaining the bit
jokes.explanation: A satisfying close to the website prank. 'You are the superior being' is funny because it's exactly what Dwight wants to hear, and the audience knows Jim typed it. The economy of the payoff is excellent.

jokes.text: Michael returns from New York unexpectedly — he pretends he 'faked out' Oscar, then Stanley, listing everyone who thought he was gone and could leave early: 'Gotcha, gotcha, gotcha.'
jokes.setup: Michael told people they could leave early because he was going to New York
jokes.punchline: He's back — and frames his own failed New York trip as a deliberate prank on the staff ('I faked Oscar out'), taking pride in a 'gotcha' that was actually his own disappointment repackaged
jokes.explanation: Michael's ability to reframe his humiliation as a triumph is one of the show's great recurring character bits. 'I think I faked Oscar out' — turning a failed party trip into a 'gotcha' is quintessential Michael self-protection. Well-executed.

jokes.text: Michael's sad talking head about Ryan: 'I'm not gonna cry over it. I did that in the car on the way home.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to maintain dignity about Ryan's dismissal of him
jokes.punchline: 'I did that in the car on the way home.' — the understatement reveals he cried in the car while also technically satisfying the 'I'm not gonna cry' claim
jokes.explanation: A deceptively simple joke with tremendous emotional and comedic weight. The structure is perfect: the 'I'm not gonna cry' declaration immediately undercut by past-tense admission. The specificity of 'in the car on the way home' is what makes it great — it's not just that he cried, it's that he's managed his schedule of vulnerability around the commute. One of the episode's best moments. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in both craft and impact.

jokes.text: Michael's party wish list includes 'something made of ice,' 'someone famous,' 'go-go dancers,' 'Al Roker,' — demanding Angela make the satellite party surpass the New York party in under an hour with a $65 budget
jokes.setup: Michael wants to throw an impromptu party that embarrasses the New York launch party
jokes.punchline: His list includes impossible elements: someone famous, go-go dancers, Al Roker specifically — all on $65 in under an hour
jokes.explanation: The escalating wish list is good Michael comedy — each item more impossible than the last, culminating in the specific 'How did they get Al Roker to come?' The $65 callback from the earlier Angela beat makes this funnier for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Michael asks Andy about Angela as a potential romantic target, spelling out 'W-O-M-A-N' to clarify he means romantically; Andy says he hadn't noticed she's a woman
jokes.setup: Michael is interested in Angela and asks Andy his opinion
jokes.punchline: Andy's claim that he 'hadn't noticed' Angela is a woman — a ridiculous denial. Michael's spelling out W-O-M-A-N as clarification adds absurdist texture.
jokes.explanation: A functional joke about Andy's obliviousness / awkward denial. The W-O-M-A-N spelling is a nice Michael touch. Not exceptional but earns its place.

jokes.text: Michael suggests Andy date Kelly since 'she works here too'; Andy says that's different because 'she works in the annex.' Michael: 'You're also welcome to date Toby.'
jokes.setup: Michael is advising Andy on dating colleagues; Andy says dating people from work is inappropriate
jokes.punchline: 'You're also welcome to date Toby.' — the most dismissive possible thing Michael can say, as if offering Toby as a consolation prize (or punishment)
jokes.explanation: Michael's Toby hatred is one of the show's most reliable comedy engines. 'You're also welcome to date Toby' works because Michael is simultaneously solving Andy's problem and insulting Toby by offering him as a last resort. The economy is superb. Pure Michael voice.

jokes.text: Kevin reveals Michael ordered from 'Pizza by Alfredo' not 'Alfredo's Pizza Cafe'; office erupts; Michael: 'What is better, a medium amount of good pizza or all you can eat of pretty good pizza?' Oscar: 'A medium amount of good pizza.' Multiple voices confirm it's bad.
jokes.setup: Michael ordered pizza for the party; Kevin reveals which of the two pizza places — one good, one terrible — he ordered from
jokes.punchline: It's the bad one ('Pizza by Alfredo'); Michael's false equivalence ('pretty good pizza' vs. 'good pizza') is immediately rejected; Oscar: 'A medium amount of good pizza.' Multiple people: 'It's like eating a hot circle of garbage.'
jokes.explanation: 'A hot circle of garbage' is one of the episode's most quotable lines — perfectly economical, viscerally descriptive. The 'Alfredo's Pizza Cafe vs. Pizza by Alfredo' distinction is a great worldbuilding joke that The Office fans know well. The group's immediate and unanimous rejection of Michael's 'pretty good pizza' rationalization is structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: Michael has ordered Pizza by Alfredo instead of Alfredo's Pizza Cafe. When told they're the same thing: extended debate about quality, ending in: 'It's like eating a hot circle of garbage.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to pass off the wrong pizza place as the right one; everyone is debating whether they're the same
jokes.punchline: 'It's like eating a hot circle of garbage' — someone's (Oscar's?) verdict on Pizza by Alfredo, delivered with genuine revulsion
jokes.explanation: 'A hot circle of garbage' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode and arguably one of the most memorable pizza-related insults in TV comedy. The word 'circle' is the key — 'hot garbage' is common, but 'hot CIRCLE of garbage' captures the exact shape and temperature of bad pizza with absurdist precision. Immediately memorable, instantly usable in real life. High quotability.

jokes.text: Andy to Angela while she works: 'You looking for dinner and a movie? You're not gonna find it in that box. It just so happens I know where you can find it, but again... Not in the box.'
jokes.setup: Andy is making his move on Angela; she's ignoring him entirely while working
jokes.punchline: His flirtation is awkward, circular, and entirely unrequested — 'Not in the box' repeated as if it's a charming callback to himself
jokes.explanation: Andy's awkward pickup attempts on Angela are good cringe comedy. The 'Not in the box' repeated as his own self-congratulatory callback is very Andy — he's genuinely proud of the line. Character-specific and uncomfortable in the right way.

jokes.text: Angela's overwhelmed talking head: lists all her problems — new party in an hour, no number two, no one for orchids/chocolates/ice thing — and ends with: 'And my upper back itched all day, and I can't reach it. And Kevin had Greek food for lunch again.'
jokes.setup: Angela is cataloging her genuine professional grievances
jokes.punchline: The list ends with two personal grievances of wildly diminishing professional relevance — her unreachable back itch and Kevin's Greek food
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured escalation-and-pivot. The professional complaints are legitimate; 'my upper back itched all day and I can't reach it' pivots to personal discomfort; 'Kevin had Greek food for lunch again' is the perfect absurdist button — it's not even Angela's problem except that she can apparently smell it. The descending relevance structure mirrors id:22 ('your cat's still dead') but works differently. Excellent Angela characterization.

jokes.text: Andy to Michael: 'They say you should never mix business with pleasure. Really? Well then explain to me how a putt-putt golf company operates.'
jokes.setup: Andy is justifying his pursuit of Angela (a coworker) to Michael
jokes.punchline: His counter-argument is putt-putt golf — a business that is literally built on fun. The logic almost works, which is what makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever piece of absurdist logic. The putt-putt golf argument is funny because it sort of works — putt-putt IS business and pleasure mixed. Andy's earnest delivery of this as a genuine philosophical rebuttal is perfect. Quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael argues with the pizza delivery kid over the half-off coupon that isn't applying to his eight-pizza order; the kid: 'Great story.'
jokes.setup: Michael ordered eight pizzas expecting a half-off coupon to apply; the delivery kid says it only applies to two-pizza orders
jokes.punchline: Michael's indignant speech about policy being on the coupon ends with the kid's flat 'Great story.' — teenage dismissal vs. adult authority
jokes.explanation: 'Great story' as a teenage dismissal of Michael's earnest lecture is a good moment. The power dynamic — adult manager vs. delivery kid who doesn't care — is a good comedy engine. Sets up the kidnapping escalation.

jokes.text: Michael detains the pizza delivery kid: 'You are not going anywhere. You're going to stay here until we figure this out.' Then escalates: 'This young man needs to learn that's not how you treat people.' Then asks Dwight to escort him to the conference room.
jokes.setup: The coupon dispute has reached an impasse
jokes.punchline: Michael's response to a routine business disagreement is to detain the delivery kid as a teaching moment, escalating a pizza coupon dispute into a hostage situation
jokes.explanation: The escalation of a petty coupon dispute into false imprisonment is a great Michael premise. 'This young man needs to learn that's not how you treat people' — Michael framing his illegal detention as a life lesson is perfectly in character. Escalates the episode's B-plot into absurdist territory.

jokes.text: 'No, you don't even know what stupid is! It's about to get all stupid up in here!'
jokes.setup: The pizza kid calls the situation 'stupid'; Michael is escalating
jokes.punchline: 'It's about to get all stupid up in here!' — Michael threatening with 'stupid' while simultaneously being the source of all the stupidity
jokes.explanation: 'It's about to get all stupid up in here' is a great Michael threat — he's threatening escalation into stupidity while being unaware that he is the stupid. Quotable and character-specific. The word 'stupid' repeated as both a threat and a self-description is good ironic structure.

jokes.text: Jim, Stanley, and Dwight researching the legality of Michael's detention: Jim: 'We think it's a straight-forward kidnapping.' Stanley: 'Could you look up accomplices?' Jim/Dwight: 'We're looking up jail time.'
jokes.setup: The office has realized Michael has detained the pizza kid and is now researching their collective legal exposure
jokes.punchline: Their research has organized naturally by crime severity — Jim on the main charge, Dwight/Jim on accomplice liability, Stanley on 'accomplices' — treating it as a routine office task
jokes.explanation: The coordination of the office's legal research — each person assigned a different crime to look up — is excellently structured. 'We think it's a straightforward kidnapping' said with the same tone as 'We think Q3 projections are up' is a great deadpan. The collective normalization of the felony is the joke.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I've seen this kid — he sneaks onto my farm and steals my hemp.' Jim: 'Yeah, I know that guy. He's that farmer that grows really crappy weed.'
jokes.setup: Dwight identifies the pizza kid as someone he knows
jokes.punchline: Jim has apparently heard of Dwight's hemp farm — as a local producer of 'really crappy weed'
jokes.explanation: A perfect two-line joke. Dwight having a hemp farm is funny; Jim knowing Dwight's hemp farm by reputation as producing 'really crappy weed' is a great additional layer — it implies the whole Scranton community is aware of Dwight's sideline and has evaluated its quality. The specificity of 'really crappy weed' is excellent. High character integration for both — only Jim would know this about Dwight.

jokes.text: Michael tries to intimidate the detained pizza kid: 'You ready to give me my discount now?' Kid: 'No.' Michael: 'What have you done in here this whole time? What kind of business is this?' Kid: 'A paper company.' Dwight: 'The best paper company in the whole wide world!'
jokes.setup: Michael confronts the kid to extract a confession/discount
jokes.punchline: Dwight's completely unsolicited, enthusiastic defense of Dunder Mifflin's quality while Michael is trying to conduct an intimidation interrogation
jokes.explanation: Dwight's 'The best paper company in the whole wide world!' delivered mid-interrogation is a great character moment — Dwight's loyalty to Dunder Mifflin is so reflexive it erupts even at completely inappropriate moments. Michael's 'Knock it off' is a good button.

jokes.text: Michael to pizza kid: 'You're a little snot-nose punk kid who thinks he's better than everybody else. Because he's some hotshot. And you don't know anything about sales.' Kid: 'You're such a loser.' Michael: 'What did you call him?' Dwight: 'A loser.' Michael: 'What did you say?!' Dwight: 'A loser.' Michael: 'Stop getting him to say it!'
jokes.setup: Michael is berating the pizza kid; the kid calls Michael a loser
jokes.punchline: Michael asks Dwight to confirm what was said — Dwight repeats 'a loser' twice — and Michael yells at Dwight to stop making him say it, as if repetition is the problem
jokes.explanation: 'Stop getting him to say it!' is a brilliant escalation. Michael makes the problem worse by having Dwight repeat the insult, then blames Dwight for the repetition. The structure is tight: setup (kid insults Michael) → escalation (Michael asks for confirmation) → misfired punchline (Dwight keeps saying it) → Michael's completely illogical blame of Dwight. One of the stronger moments in the kidnapping sequence.

jokes.text: Jim: 'We are accomplices.' Dwight: 'Stop talking all at once.' Jim: 'You need to let him go.' Michael: 'Let go of little jerk boy? Before he has learned his lesson?' Jim: 'Yes.' Michael: 'I'm not kidnapping him. I'm keeping him until I get what I want. As a hostage.' Jim: 'You over-think it.' Michael: 'You under-think it.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to get Michael to release the pizza kid; Michael refuses to see this as kidnapping
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not kidnapping him. I'm keeping him until I get what I want. As a hostage.' Then Jim: 'You over-think it.' Michael: 'You under-think it.' — the philosophical exchange between them about the definition of kidnapping
jokes.explanation: 'You over-think it. / You under-think it.' is possibly the episode's most quotable exchange. Michael's distinction between 'kidnapping' and 'keeping someone until I get what I want as a hostage' is a perfect Michael logic loop — he thinks re-labeling changes the crime. Jim's 'You over-think it' is a masterful straight-man line, and Michael's 'You under-think it' retort completes the joke with flawless symmetry. Approaches the episode's top tier.

jokes.text: Michael calls Alfredo's to negotiate: 'Could you tell the manager that I am keeping his delivery kid until I get my discount on the eight pizzas I ordered?' Then adds: 'Also I would like him to throw in two — three pizzas just for our... [Jim: Ransom.] ...trouble.'
jokes.setup: Michael is negotiating with the pizza place via phone while holding their delivery kid hostage
jokes.punchline: He escalates his demands to include bonus pizzas 'for our trouble' — Jim supplies the word 'ransom' which Michael was avoiding, completing the criminal framing
jokes.explanation: The negotiation escalating to include ransom pizzas is a good extension of the kidnapping premise. Jim supplying 'ransom' while Michael was trying to avoid the word is a nice beat — Jim naming the crime Michael is committing while Michael searches for euphemism. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Michael to the pizza kid: 'I don't like you, but because some town in Switzerland says so, you have rights.'
jokes.setup: Michael is addressing the detained pizza kid and apparently deciding to respect his rights
jokes.punchline: 'Some town in Switzerland says so' — Michael's vague understanding of the Geneva Convention (which applies to prisoners of war, not pizza delivery disputes) as the source of human rights
jokes.explanation: One of the great Michael Scott lines. 'Some town in Switzerland says so' — his half-remembered invocation of the Geneva Convention, filtered through complete ignorance of what it actually says and when it applies — is perfect. It's funny as a misapplication of international law to a pizza coupon dispute. It's funnier that he's citing it in the context of a hostage situation he created. And the grudging 'I don't like you, but...' makes it poignant and absurd simultaneously. Near-perfect economy. One of the episode's top three lines.

jokes.text: Andy notices Dwight staring at Angela and confronts him: 'Why are you looking at her like that? Hey!'
jokes.setup: Andy is pursuing Angela; Dwight is watching Angela with evident longing
jokes.punchline: Andy's territorial confrontation of Dwight — 'Hey!' — over a woman neither of them is supposed to be involved with, creating a love triangle that Angela is not participating in
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the developing Andy/Dwight/Angela triangle. The reaction beat of Andy confronting Dwight over eye contact is funny primarily because Angela is completely unaware. Mostly setup; the comedy is situational.

jokes.text: The office discovers Michael's hostage situation and orders good pizza from Alfredo's Pizza Cafe to eat while waiting for the bad pizza hostage crisis to resolve
jokes.setup: The office is hungry; the bad pizza (Pizza by Alfredo) is being held as part of the hostage negotiation
jokes.punchline: The office orders GOOD pizza (Alfredo's Pizza Cafe) to eat while waiting for the BAD pizza hostage situation to end — they've just accepted the kidnapping and moved on to logistics
jokes.explanation: The office's pragmatic response to the kidnapping — ordering better pizza to eat while they wait — is a great piece of ensemble comedy. The callback to the Alfredo's/Pizza by Alfredo distinction pays off beautifully. The acceptance of the hostage situation as a background event while they solve the more pressing problem (hunger) is absurdist perfection.

jokes.text: Dwight presents Angela with 'one thing made of ice' — a full ice sculpture, apparently stolen — Angela: 'How did you... Where did you...?' Dwight: 'I stole it.'
jokes.setup: Michael's impossible party wish list included 'something made of ice'; Angela couldn't deliver this
jokes.punchline: Dwight has produced a full ice sculpture — and when Angela asks how, he flatly says 'I stole it.' — no context, no hesitation, complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: 'I stole it.' — two words that are the entire joke. The build of Angela's astonishment ('How did you... Where did you...') followed by the flat confession is structurally perfect. The deadpan delivery with zero shame is pure Dwight. The ice sculpture is presumably in the background as a visual gag. One of the episode's most economical and satisfying moments.

jokes.text: Michael takes the good pizza to the roof with Jim's help — Michael: 'If I take a pizza, do you think you could take some sodas and some napkins up to the roof?' Jim: 'I'm all over it.'
jokes.setup: Michael has returned from New York humiliated and is now managing the party situation
jokes.punchline: Michael absconding to the roof with the good pizza — a kind of Michael self-exile with snacks — Jim's enthusiastic 'I'm all over it' implies he's genuinely happy for the escape
jokes.explanation: A gentle scene beat more than a joke — Michael retreating to the roof is funny as a character behavior but the dialogue is minimal. 'I'm all over it' from Jim implies he's also glad to escape, which is a small bonus.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam on the roof: Jim recalls his first day — Pam's memory of the moment she knew she liked Jim: 'That mixed berry yogurt you're about to eat has expired.' Jim: 'That was the moment that you knew you liked me?' Pam: 'Yep.' Jim: 'Can we make it a different moment?' Pam: 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are sharing the tender memory of when they first knew they liked each other
jokes.punchline: Pam's moment of falling for Jim was him warning her about expired yogurt — mundane, prosaic, deeply unromantic — and she refuses to change it
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most emotionally resonant joke and one of its best-crafted. The setup invites a romantic revelation; the punchline is expired yogurt. But what makes it exceptional is that Pam's answer is genuine — it's not a funny story to her, it was a real moment of connection. Jim's 'Can we make it a different moment?' and Pam's flat 'Nope' is perfect. The comedy emerges from the truth of the relationship — Jim's small kindness about yogurt was real, and Pam recognized it as who he was. Deeply character-specific and structurally beautiful. Among the episode's very best.

jokes.text: Michael is introduced on the New York webcam by Ryan and immediately says: 'I just think you should know that one of my salesmen beat your stupid computer. So take that, asshole.' Ryan: 'Always a jokester.'
jokes.setup: Ryan introduces Michael on the webcam as part of the formal launch party broadcast
jokes.punchline: Michael's entire live statement is an insult aimed at Ryan's computer; Ryan saves face with 'Always a jokester' — pretending it's a joke rather than a genuine attack
jokes.explanation: Already scored as id:54 in the competition context, but this is the full broadcast version with Ryan's save. 'Always a jokester' is a great institutional denial — Ryan pretending Michael's live insult was a prepared bit. The relief in Ryan's voice (implied) vs. the reality of Michael's sincerity is the comedy.

jokes.text: Pizza kid hijacks the webcam and says to the whole company: 'If anyone out there is listening, I'm being held here against my will. I'm a minor.'
jokes.setup: The office's webcam is live during the launch party broadcast
jokes.punchline: The pizza kid uses the live company-wide broadcast to announce his detention — his plea for rescue is seen by every branch
jokes.explanation: The kid's escape attempt via the company webcam is a great escalation of the kidnapping plot. 'I'm a minor' as his final credential is a nice touch — he's invoking his age as added legal protection. The structural payoff of the webcam (established as a key plot device) being used by the hostage is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Andy scratches Angela's upper back for her — she hasn't asked for this; she reacts with 'I didn't ask you to scratch it' — Andy explains his feelings; Angela: 'I'm not dating you.'
jokes.setup: Angela mentioned her back itch in her talking head (id:67); Andy apparently overheard or noticed and is now scratching it unsolicited
jokes.punchline: The unsolicited back scratch as a romantic overture; Angela's flat 'I'm not dating you' in response to his confession
jokes.explanation: The callback to Angela's back itch paying off as Andy's romantic gesture is a satisfying structural close. The comedy is in the intimate intrusion of the scratch and Angela's immediate clinical rejection. Character-specific for both — Andy's awkward earnestness and Angela's emotional unavailability.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head about pursuing Angela: 'So Angela is stubborn as a mule... She's giving off fairly strong vibes that she's not interested... But do I like her or not? Because if I like her, then I can't back down.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been rejected by Angela
jokes.punchline: His logic: if he likes her, rejection is irrelevant — he 'can't back down.' The anti-logic of persistence despite overwhelming signals is both funny and a perfect Andy character beat.
jokes.explanation: 'Stubborn as a mule' is a great Angela descriptor. Andy's reasoning — that his own feelings override her complete lack of interest — is simultaneously infuriating and funny. Good character work for Andy's particular brand of oblivious determination.

jokes.text: Michael: 'If you're going number one, you've got ten more seconds!' — apparently to the pizza kid in the conference room
jokes.setup: The pizza kid is being held in the conference room
jokes.punchline: Michael is apparently regulating the kid's bathroom breaks — 'ten more seconds' for urination implies he's timing it, turning the hostage situation into a grade-school power dynamic
jokes.explanation: 'If you're going number one, you've got ten more seconds!' — said to a kidnapping victim — perfectly captures Michael's relationship with authority. He's treating a felony like a field trip. The specificity of 'number one' is the right level of absurdist detail. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight tries to intimidate the pizza kid by pretending he's going to do something to him — 'The trick is to make him think you're gonna do something to him' — the kid: 'I can hear you, man.' Dwight: 'Shut up! Or I punch you in the throat!'
jokes.setup: Dwight is running a good-cop/bad-cop interrogation approach — explaining his method while the kid is still in the room
jokes.punchline: The kid points out he can hear Dwight explaining the technique; Dwight's response is to threaten a throat punch
jokes.explanation: The meta-failure of the interrogation technique (explaining it in front of the subject) is a good Dwight moment. 'Or I punch you in the throat!' as the response to being caught is very Dwight — doubling down rather than adjusting. 'I can hear you, man' is a perfect deadpan teen line.

jokes.text: Michael's guilt spiral: 'Oh my god. I kidnapped a kid.' Dwight: 'You had to. What other choice did you have?' Michael: 'I've gotta pay for the pizza.' Dwight: 'Well... Yeah.' Michael: 'Oh my god.'
jokes.setup: Michael has a moment of clarity about what he's done
jokes.punchline: Dwight's validation — 'You had to. What other choice did you have?' — and his eventual reluctant agreement that Michael should pay for the pizza reveals that even Dwight has limits
jokes.explanation: 'You had to. What other choice did you have?' is a great Dwight line — completely sincere, completely wrong. The conversation's arc from Dwight's validation to his quiet agreement that Michael should pay is a good micro-structure. Two people gradually realizing they've committed a felony over pizza is good comedy.

jokes.text: Ryan calls Michael: 'First off, thanks for the shout-out.' Michael pretends to have a bad connection: 'You're breaking up. I can't hear you.' Ryan: 'Why's there a kid on your web cam saying he's being held against his...'
jokes.setup: Ryan has seen the pizza kid's appeal on the webcam and is calling to ask about it
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately fakes a bad connection when confronted about the kidnapping — then Ryan is cut off mid-sentence exactly at the word 'against his...' which is probably funnier than any completed accusation
jokes.explanation: Michael's fake-connection dodge is a classic avoidance maneuver, and the timing of Ryan being cut off at 'against his...' is a good structural choice. The 'thanks for the shout-out' opening from Ryan (acknowledging Michael's 'asshole' comment as a joke) is a nice continuing thread.

jokes.text: Michael instructs Dwight on the pizza release plan: 'I will open the door. And hopefully, he will walk out. And the rest is out of our hands.'
jokes.setup: Michael has decided to pay and release the pizza kid
jokes.punchline: 'The rest is out of our hands.' — Michael's plan for releasing his hostage is to open a door and hope — treating the consequences of his own actions as an external force beyond his control
jokes.explanation: 'The rest is out of our hands' is a perfect Michael line — he commits a crime, fixes it as minimally as possible, and then treats the outcome as a divine mystery. The passive construction removes his agency from a situation he entirely created. Very high economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Michael pays the delivery kid $65 full price, then: 'You know what? Here's two more.' — adds $2 tip. Kid leaves. Michael: 'See ya. Drive safely.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been talked into paying full price; he adds a small tip
jokes.punchline: A $2 tip on a $65 pizza order after detaining the kid as a hostage — and then the cheerful 'Drive safely' sendoff as if this was a normal transaction
jokes.explanation: 'Drive safely' after a kidnapping is a great closer for the hostage arc. The $2 tip is appropriately insulting. Michael's breezy sendoff perfectly characterizes how quickly he processes moral guilt and returns to normalcy.

jokes.text: Office toast: 'To avoiding a class 2 felony charge.'
jokes.setup: The pizza hostage situation has been resolved; someone proposes a toast
jokes.punchline: 'To avoiding a class 2 felony charge.' — a toast that requires them to have nearly committed a serious crime as a prerequisite for celebration
jokes.explanation: A perfect button for the kidnapping subplot. The specificity of 'class 2 felony' — implying someone looked it up (which we know Stanley did) — and the dark normalcy of toasting to its avoidance is excellent. Economy is near-perfect: six words close the entire arc. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Andy serenades Angela with ABBA's 'Take a Chance on Me' — performed sincerely, with full commitment — ending with: 'That's all I ask of you, Angela.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been rejected by Angela and is making one final romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: He performs 'Take a Chance on Me' earnestly and in full — the ABBA choice, the sincerity, and Angela's visible discomfort create sustained cringe comedy; his final personalization 'That's all I ask of you, Angela' is both absurd and almost touching
jokes.explanation: The ABBA serenade is the episode's cringe peak. Andy's commitment to the performance — the whole song, earnestly — is exactly what makes it both uncomfortable and funny. The choice of ABBA (cheesy, sincere, impossible to perform un-ironically but Andy manages) is perfect character work. Angela's frozen-in-place reaction is the implied visual punch. 'That's all I ask of you, Angela' personalizing the lyric is a great closer. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Michael's final talking head: 'What a horrible day.' Then a long pause. 'Well, I need to get the horrible taste of this pizza out of my mouth. I'd really like some sushi.'
jokes.setup: Michael reflects on his terrible day — rejected by Ryan, missed the party, ran a hostage situation
jokes.punchline: His reflection on the day's horror pivots entirely to the pizza's taste; he decides he deserves New York sushi — and will get it tonight despite everything
jokes.explanation: Michael processing a day of professional humiliation and emotional pain through the lens of pizza quality is very him. The pivot from 'horrible day' to 'horrible pizza' to 'I want sushi' is a good character moment — Michael's resilience via self-indulgence. Ends the episode on the right note.

jokes.text: Michael decides he needs New York-style sushi and declares 'there's only one place to get New York-style sushi' — someone suggests Tokyo; Michael says 'New York.' They go to New York for sushi.
jokes.setup: Michael is disappointed after his failed New York trip
jokes.punchline: He decides to make the trip again — this time for sushi — and rejects Tokyo as the source of New York-style sushi in favor of New York, which he just came from
jokes.explanation: Decent ending gag. Michael's decision to go back to New York immediately after a disastrous trip there — for sushi — is funny as character comedy. Jim's apparent willingness to drive him is the real joke.

jokes.text: Michael and Jim end up at the New York nightclub after all — Michael is recognized: 'Hey, you're the Scranton guy. Guilty.' 'This is the guy that beat the computer.' 'It was funny to see Ryan all embarrassed by that.'
jokes.setup: Michael went to New York for sushi and ends up at the actual launch party — he's been accidentally vindicated
jokes.punchline: Michael is a celebrity at the party not for any of the reasons he planned, but because of his 'asshole' webcam moment and Dwight's computer victory — the things he did accidentally are what got him in the door
jokes.explanation: A satisfying ironic closing — Michael's accidental moments of authenticity have made him famous at the party he was excluded from. The structural payoff of the 'asshole' webcam line finally working for Michael is good. 'Guilty' as his response to being IDed is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Ryan's final drunk/humiliated talking head: 'I'm Ryan, and tonight didn't go the way I thought it would... I have egg all over my face. And I'm 12 years old. I spent so much time in Scranton, but I never sold any paper. I started a fire with my cheese peeler. And dated an Indian girl. I started a fire. Now I got a beard. And I have new shoes and I'm your boss. I'm hot. I'm so hot. That's why everybody-- I don't get-- I don't understand that. That's part of it.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is drunk at the end of his humiliating launch party and giving a final talking head
jokes.punchline: His self-assessment is a chaotic stream of confession, self-aggrandizement, and collapse — 'I started a fire with my cheese peeler' alongside 'I'm so hot' — the jumble reveals his complete psychological unraveling
jokes.explanation: Ryan's end-of-episode breakdown is a tour de force character comedy moment. The stream-of-consciousness mixing of self-pity ('I never sold any paper'), ancient callbacks ('I started a fire with my cheese peeler'), and delusional self-promotion ('I'm so hot') is a perfect encapsulation of his character's collapse. 'And dated an Indian girl' landing with the same weight as 'I started a fire' is a great structural choice. The Season 1 callback ('started a fire') is a rich reward for long-term viewers. One of the episode's best character moments.

tmdb_overview: Michael gleefully anticipates attending the company's Web-site launch party in New York. Meanwhile, Angela arranges a bash in Scranton, while Dwight gets wrapped up in a real paper chase: He tries to sell more paper than the Web site.
